morph.elicq: Cojocaru 2003 gives citation words with syllable-by-syllable stress marks and minimal pairs, no method stated: 'The stress can fall on any syllable of the word: ─ ┴ ca-fea coffee; ┴ ─ ca-să house ... CVC sequences (tokir), CVVC sequences with light diphthongs (puer), CVV sequences with heavy diphthongs'; 'incomplete-phase words all end in a stressed heavy syllable'; 'heavy syllables are limited to final position'. 748.heavy: Any final syllable whose nucleus is not the high central vowel /ɨ/ attracts (word) stress; a final syllable containing /ɨ/ repels it to the penult. 748.prule: Word stress (Guy's 'secondary stress'): on the final syllable of the word, unless that syllable contains the vowel /ɨ/, in which case on the penultimate. Monosyllabic particles usually unstressed.

753.prule: 'Phonetic accentuation rule': stress stands on the long vowel nearest the end of the word; if the non-first syllables contain no long vowel, stress is on the first syllable. Holds for unaffixed words and words with 'first-kind' affixes (most nominal affixes, infinitive, single-consonant affixes, monosyllabic affixes with у); 'second-kind' affixes (few; e.g. verbal -oĺ, -aĺ) carry a short vowel treated as long by the rule; 'third-kind' affixes make the word form double-stressed; 2Sg imperative forms fall outside the rule (root-dependent, archaic).
753.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress is described. A second stress arises only morphologically: 'third-kind' affixes make the word form double-stressed (двуударная словоформа), the affix bearing a stress in addition to the one placed by the long-vowel rule, e.g. tɨ̄·lɔ̄· 'closer hither', tɛ·nɨsɨ·mil' 'clever' (Helimski 1993:358); the two stresses are not ranked by the source.

Такое перемещение главного ударения бывает обусловлено наличием во втором слоге долгого гласного или дифтонга, при условии наличия в первом слоге краткого гласного. Напр., çattьŋьt 'он бросил' ... çattéiŋьt 'он бросил (сразу)'.» ОчСЯ 1980:138-141 (quoted in Норманская 2018:270-271) formulates the rule in terms of AFFIX classes rather than the root: «Для формулировки акцентуационных правил необходимо разграничить три…
morph.elicq: Neither Prokof'ev 1935 §3 nor the ОчСЯ 1980 passage (as quoted by Норманская 2018:270-271) says how stress placements were established. Prokof'ev's data come from residence among Taz Selkups: «Автор настоящей работы (с осени 1925 до весны 1928) заведывал первой школой среди селькупов, организованной в Яновом Стане (на р. Турухане)» (p. 15, fn. 1); the stress examples are cited as isolated word forms (çattьŋьt vs çattéiŋьt) but no elicitation procedure is stated. ОчСЯ 1980 is described only as based on «полевые исследования 1970-1973 и 1977 гг.».
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: «Принадлежа по основным своим признакам к числу самоедских языков, селькупский язык тем самым является языком агглютинирующим... суффиксы тех или иных грамматических категорий наслаиваются друг на друга в определенной последовательности» (Prokof'ev 1935, pp. 16-17; e.g. ātæ 'олень' > ātæ-n-nDь-nьk 'к его оленю'); every inflectional and derivational category in the grammar is a suffix, negation and polar interrogation are free preverbal particles, and the 64 INEL text tokens show 0 prefixes vs 58 suffixes.

754.dq: Every complete word contains at the most only one strong stress that is morphologically conditioned, although syntactic factors may add another stress when the word occurs in a complete utterance. (Chafe 1967:3)
754.dloc: Chafe 1967 Introduction (synopsis of the morphology) p.3; sec. 4.1-4.4 pp.10-11; sec. 1.1 p.5, sec. 1.18 p.6; enclitic -kwah sec. 26.8 p.33; Chafe 1977:178 (StressTyp2 carried, entry)
754.heavy: Closure, not length: an even-numbered non-final vowel attracts strong stress if it is followed (before any even prefinal vowel) by (b) a laryngeal obstruent h/?, (c) a cluster of two obstruents (1.1: 'two consonants not including n, w, or y'), or (d) s plus n or w (Chafe 1967 secs. 1.1, 4.4); Chafe 1977 restates this as 'closed syllable' or 'open syllable immediately followed by a closed syllable'. Vowel length is NOT a weight criterion (it is derived, 'complementary to stress'). Chafe 1967 adds a lexically marked class of 'basically strong' vowels (condition (a)) that pattern like closed syllables.
754.dflt: no stress/accent at all on the word (Chafe 1967:11 'many words have none'; Chafe 1977:178 'the word will bear no accent at all')
754.prule: Count vowels from the word start on basic allomorphs (sec. 4.2). Strong stress falls on the rightmost even-numbered non-final vowel that is 'basically strong' or has following it (before any even prefinal vowel) a laryngeal obstruent, an obstruent cluster, or s+n/w -- i.e. the last even-numbered non-final syllable that is closed or immediately followed by a closed syllable (Chafe 1977). An even prefinal vowel itself is stressed only if basically strong (a following ? does not count there: hoyetota:?toh). At most one strong stress per word; if nothing qualifies the word has no stress at all.
754.srule: No separate secondary stress. Chafe 1967: 'No word has more than one strong stress, and many words have none' (an extra stress may be added by syntactic factors in an utterance). Later description (Chafe 1996; 1998, as reported and adopted by Melinger 2002): every non-final even-numbered syllable that is closed or immediately followed by a closed syllable is accented with equally high pitch, so a word may carry several accents -- not necessarily at regular intervals, with no hierarchy among them (Chafe rejects the term 'secondary accent') -- or none.

755.heavy: Root-final syllable is heavy if it has a complex nucleus (long vowel or diphthong: 'two or more vowels in the nucleus') and/or a complex coda ('two or more consonants in the coda'); the root-final consonant is extrametrical, so a final syllable with a simple coda (CVC#) is light. 756.heavy: Common ground of all three sources: a second syllable closed by a consonant (coda, incl. sibilants and a nasal realised as vowel nasalisation = 'underlying nasalized vowel') is heavy and attracts stress; an initial (odd) closed syllable never outcompetes it (Elias-Ulloa: odd closed syllables 'forced to be light', contextual weight). Valenzuela et al. 2001 and Faust 1973 count only closure/nasalisation as heavy, list no vowel-length contrast (JIPA vowel chart: four oral + four nasal vowels, no length), and treat open-second-syllable-stressed words (popo, tasa, kapɯ 'alligator'; StressTyp2: ochiti, jatibi) as exceptions / 'stress distinctive'. Elias-Ulloa 2006 alone adds long vowels ((C)VV, bimoraic) as heavy, but states long vowels are 'not predictable', occur only in even syllables and always stressed (his (ka.pɨ́ː) 'crocodile' = JIPA's exception /kaˈpɯ/, same vowel in different transcription), i.e. the CVV class re-encodes the other sources' lexical-exception class as lexical length.
756.prule: Main stress on one of the first two syllables of the word: on the second syllable if it is closed (coda consonant, incl. nasal realised as vowel nasalisation), otherwise on the first; productive under suffixation (βawa vs βawã 'parrot-ERG', bake vs baken; panin-ti vs pani.n-a). A lexically listed residue has second-syllable stress on an open syllable (JIPA: 'exceptions', 'stress must be considered distinctive'; Faust: 'some exceptions'; Elias-Ulloa: unpredictable long vowel in the even syllable). Initial closed syllables never outcompete a heavy second syllable; monosyllabic (long-vowel) roots stressed. Stressed syllable carries high pitch.
756.srule: Rhythmic secondary stresses (Elias-Ulloa 2006 only): after the main-stress foot the word is parsed into disyllabic feet left to right; in each foot the second syllable is stressed if it has a long vowel or is closed, otherwise the first (trochaic by default); a leftover final odd syllable is unstressed; heavy syllables never surface unstressed. Diagnosed by resistance to vowel laxing/devoicing and high tone on long vowels; 'not necessarily audible'.

tn.quote: Abbasi (2015b) argues on Sindhi as a language in which intonation contours appear to be independent of stress. It suggests that stress is completely orthogonal to F0 contours unlike in most stress languages in which pitch accents dock on stressed syllables. Sindhi pitch accent rises from the first syllable string in disyllable words, regardless of syllable heaviness, and the rise is trailed by a fall at end of the word. Thus, the study suggests that Sindhi seems to behave like a stress accent language.

tn.note: Pitch described as intonational: a rise from the first syllable and a word-final fall regardless of syllable weight, independent of stress; Sindhi classed as a stress-accent language. No lexical tone.

758.cfw: Khubchandani's own account (1961 thesis, 1969 article, 2003 handbook chapter) sets out a detailed weight-sensitive rule with examples, a lone heavy syllable takes primary stress wherever it sits, otherwise the last non-final heavy syllable, and all-light words stress the penult, and Abbasi and Hussain 2015 and Abbasi et al. 2018 independently find weakly quantity-sensitive rather than fixed stress, so Nihalani's 1999 one-sentence claim of fixed initial stress stands alone against them, though Abbasi et al. 2018 concede that the very existence of Sindhi word stress is still contested.

evidence_works.work: Simonović & Kager 2023, Avoiding stress on non-lexical material in nouns and verbs: predictable verb prosody in Serbo-Croatian stress standard varieties (Linguistics 61(5): 1105-1130)
evidence_works.detail: Published form of the 2017 OCP talk. States that the standard language has two prosodic implementations: 'Standard Serbo-Croatian has two groups of varieties that differ in prosody. On the one hand, there are pitch-accent varieties with contrastive vowel length, spoken in what is traditionally considered the Neo-Štokavian dialect area (e.g., in Osijek, Zadar, Split, Novi Sad and Belgrade). On the other hand, there are stress varieties without contrastive vowel length, spoken in cities in what are traditionally considered Old-Štokavian and Non-Štokavian dialect areas (e.g., in Zagreb, Rijeka, Pula, Niš, Zaječar and Bor)' (p. 1107); pitch-accent speakers say pogledamo 'we look' as [ˈpoglédaːmo] 'with stress on the first syllable, high tone on the second, and a long third syllable', stress speakers as [poˈgledamo] (p. 1107). 'In stress standard SC the stress position in verbs is predictable [...] As a first approximation, we can say that verbal stress in stress standard SC is typically stem-final. [...] Noun prosody, on the other hand, is contrastive in all varieties' (p. 1108; ˈnóvine/noˈviné vs stress-standard ˈnovine/noˈvine 'newspapers'/'novelties'); 'pitch-accent standard SC has lexical prosody in both nouns and verbs, whereas stress standard SC only has lexical prosody in nouns, but not in verbs' (p. 1108). Material and procedure: 'a database of the 3,000 most frequent verbs in the Serbian variety of standard Serbo-Croatian', drawn from 'the web corpus srWac (Ljubešić and Klubička 2014)'; 'We asked four stress standard SC speakers (two from Niš, one from Bor and one from Zaječar) to pronounce one finite and one non-finite form of each verb', using 'the variety they would speak when talking to a stranger from their own hometown in a relatively formal setting (e.g., at a doctor's or a government office)' (p. 1111, section 3.2 Dataset; dataset on Zenodo, fn. 2, p. 1111). The article's own data are for the Serbian stress standard (Niš, Bor, Zaječar); the Zagreb/Croatian stress standard is characterised by reference to Kapović 2018 and the authors' 2017/2020 remarks.

It argues from a prosodic alternation in derived nouns: nominalisations 'which the authors analyse as part of the paradigm of the base adjective/verb copy the prosodic pattern of the base, while the nominalisations analysed as having left the paradigm of the base and having their own lexical entry display a fixed prosodic pattern – a rising span over the two final syllables' (p. 313; minimal pairs pUtovaanje 'travelling' vs putovAAnjE 'trip', Opaasnoost 'dangerousness' vs opAAsnOOst 'danger'). 'In claiming that the rising span is a post-lexical pattern, they go against the grain of most analyses of S-C prosody, according to which the only post-lexical is one with an initial falling accent' (p. 313), and the talk adds 'a very limited number of nouns which display the same rising pattern only in some fixed expressions in the Locative Singular form' (p. 313; example (2) spans pp. 313-314: na svakom korAAku 'everywhere' vs na petom kOraaku 'at the fifth step'). The examples are the authors' own; no elicitation procedure, speaker sample or measurement is described in the abstract.

evidence_works.work: Yu 2008, The prosody of second position clitics and focus in Zagreb Croatian (MA thesis, UCLA: 163 pp.)
evidence_works.detail: An instrumental study of focus intonation and second-position clitic placement, not of lexical accent: 'Four speakers of Zagreb Croatian living in Los Angeles and ranging in age from 39 to 61 were recorded' (S1-S4; 'all grew up in Zagreb speaking only Standard Croatian and Zagreb dialect at home'; emigrated 'about 15-17 years ago'; pp. 22-23, Table 2.1); they produced question-answer pairs with an initially stressed target word of 1-4 syllables in a 9-11-syllable carrier sentence under broad and narrow (corrective) focus, 144 sentences per speaker (section 3.1.1, pp. 78-79); tonal landmarks L1, H1 and L2 and segmentation landmarks (onset of the target word, offset of its stressed syllable, offset of the target word, offset of the clitic string, onset of the stressed syllable of the following word) were labelled and alignment analysed by nonparametric Spearman rank-order correlations and repeated-measures ANOVAs for FOCUS and WORD LENGTH (section 3.1.2, p. 81; Table 3.2, p. 82). On the accent system it restates others: 'BCS has four lexical pitch accents, traditionally categorized by the phonemic length of the stressed vowel and tonal alignment; they are called the short rise, short fall, long rise, and long fall (Godjevac 2000a, Smiljanic 2004). Smiljanic (2004) found Zagreb speakers to neutralize lexical pitch accent contrasts'. Its own first-hand addition is the register-conditioned stress position of loanwords in the stress variety: 'In colloquial Zagreb dialect, the words have noninitial stress, but in formal speech, they are initially stressed, e.g. ma"larija vs. "malarija 'malaria' or i"ronija vs. "ironija 'irony'' (p. 81), with the note that 'Two of the speakers, S3 and S4, were unable to comfortably produce two of the four syllable items with initial stress, malarija and ironija' (fn. 1, p. 81); further noninitially stressed target words me"ni 'menu', alu"minij 'aluminium', mari"nada 'marinade' (p. 80).

764.dq: Words can be differentiated only by the place of the stress. ... All disyllabic nouns and verbs bear one strong stress
764.heavy: No weight criterion stated anywhere in the reachable text; StressTyp2's own field for the Grebo lect reads 'lexical marking'.
764.prule: Each disyllabic noun/verb bears one 'strong' stress whose position (front vs back syllable) is not predictable: words are distinguished solely by the place of stress (e.g. 'sono 'sting' vs so'no 'smell'), independently of tone; the realised position further depends on style of pronunciation (Unemphatic, Emphatic 1, Emphatic 2), some words being back-stressed in UP/EP1 but front-stressed in EP2.
764.srule: None: Innes recognises only two degrees of stress, 'strong' (maximal) and 'zero', and states that 'All disyllabic nouns and verbs bear one strong stress'; no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned (words longer than two syllables not covered in the text seen).

tn.quote: Grebo has a system of four tone levels; tone is not marked in Grebo writing, but in this book, where it is necessary to mark tone, this will be shown by numerals. The method of tone marking is: 1. High tone is marked with 1: kg 1 chief 2. High-mid tone is marked with 2: bi 2 beat 3. Low-mid tone is marked with 3: ya 3 bring 4. Low tone is marked with 4: pu 4 swell Gliding tones are marked with a combination of two (or, rarely, three) numerals joined by a hyphen: hu 3-2 throw ... yiba 21 face ... gbudamu 333 box
tn.cite: Innes, Gordon (1966). An Introduction to Grebo. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. [ch.2 pp.14-15, morphosyntax chapters]
tn.note: Four level tones (1 high to 4 low), one numeral per vowel; glides written as level combinations (3-2, 3-23); 1st/2nd person differ by tone; stress contrastive apart from tone (p.18). scan 'kg' garbled.

766.heavy: geminate vowel clusters (i.e. long/identical vowel sequences) attract primary stress; closed syllables are not mentioned as stress-attracting (e.g. 'my forehead', 'my lip' with final closed syllable take penult stress). 766.prule: Primary stress on the vowel of a monosyllable and on the penultimate vowel of a polysyllable; words containing a geminate vowel cluster are stressed on that cluster (all cited cases word-final: 'quick', 'his chest', 'to clean'); residual exceptions are lexically marked with an acute accent in the vocabulary.
766.srule: Nouns: secondary stress on every alternate syllable to the left of the primary stress (syllables with epenthetic [ə]/[ɨ] count). Verbs and adjectives: secondary stress on the initial syllable and on every alternate syllable to its right, except that the syllable immediately before the primary stress is always unstressed. No weight condition on secondary stress (Nɨvhaal dialect; said to hold for Nelpwaai).

morph.stmt: Lynch §3.1 p.11: 'Verb morphology is far more complicated than the morphology of other word classes, with a verb being able to take up to seven ranks of prefixes and three ranks of suffixes, all forming a single phonological word. Person-of-subject, number-of-subject, and various tenses, aspects, and modes are indicated by prefixes; transitivity, direction, reciprocality, and some other features are indicated by suffixes.' Nouns are largely uninflected apart from possessor suffixes on directly possessed nouns and an n-/nɨ- plural prefix on some human nouns; case relations are preposed clitic case-markers -- i.e. a predominantly prefixing verb with a smaller suffixal/postclitic zone.

768.dq: All native Southeastern Tepehuan words are accented on one of the first two syllables of the stem ... The two prosodies generally coincide, except in connected discourse, where the pitch of a syllable is further influenced by intonation patterns.
768.heavy: HEAVY = a closed syllable with a short vowel, or a syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong; LIGHT = an open syllable with a short vowel (two degrees only on the surface; fn. 10 notes E. Willett 1982 posited three degrees for a derivational-stage rule)
768.prule: Accent falls on one of the first two syllables of the STEM: the heavier of the two; if equally heavy (or both light), the first. Equivalently: the first heavy syllable within the first two stem syllables, else the first syllable.
768.srule: None: one accent per word, no secondary or rhythmic stresses -- 'sólo hay un acento por palabra' (p. 180), 'la lengua no tiene acentos secundarios' (p. 190), accent 'no iterativo... sólo un acento por palabra y por lo tanto sólo un pie' (p. 195) (Reyes Taboada 2014). Willett 1991 sec. 2.31-2.32 (pp. 21-24) gives the single stem accent only and does not mention secondary stress.

769.srule: Secondary stress falls on every long (heavy: CV· or CVC) syllable after the one bearing primary stress, including the word-final syllable, which is always long; within a run of long syllables the even-numbered ones (counted from the start of the run) tend to be less heavily stressed than the odd-numbered ones; short CV syllables carry only weak stress.

morph.rootq: Rule itself is purely weight-based (sec. 140, p. 16): "Stress, which is not phonemic, can be predicted from the pattern of long and short syllables within the word. ... In isolated forms, primary stress falls on the first long syllable." But the morphemics chapter ties it to the root (sec. 220, p. 34): "Since one of the first two syllables of a word is always a long syllable bearing primary stress, this is usually part of the root." Also p. 41: particles "meet the phonological criteria for words (see section 160), each having a primary stress on the first long syllable."
morph.elicq: p. 16: "In isolated forms, primary stress falls on the first long syllable." p. 17: "In forms given in isolation—that is, before final juncture—the syllable bearing primary stress is on level 2 ... In my early attempts to record the language, I found it very easy to confuse this late high pitch with primary stress"; and "When I was being excessively dense as to the proper pronunciation of a particular form, the informant would say it very slowly, separating the syllables and enunciating each one with great care." (Impressionistic fieldwork on elicited forms; no instrumental measurement.)
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: "Each word contains, as its first morpheme, one member of the class of roots, and only one. Except in the case of particles (see section 290), the root is always followed by one or more suffixes. All words except particles end with a member of the class of final suffixes (see section 240), or with a final suffix followed by one or more postfixes" (sec. 210, p. 33); "A root is the first morpheme of a word, and occurs in no other position; a suffix is always preceded by a root" (sec. 220, p. 33). The only two morpheme distribution classes are ROOTS and SUFFIXES; there are no prefixes.
